profile.name: Rueda de Casino
profile.tagline: A Cuban round dance where couples rotate and switch partners on a caller's command.
profile.insight: Danced in circles to live salsa or timba, Rueda de Casino relies on a caller who dances inside the ring rather than shouting from the sidelines.
profile.profile: Rueda de Casino is a salsa round dance that originated in Havana, Cuba, in the early 1950s at venues like the Club Casino Deportivo. Couples form a circle and execute synchronized figures called out spontaneously by a leader, known as the cantante or líder, who dances within the group. The dance integrates elements of Cuban Son, Cha Cha Cha, Mambo, and Rumba, and features continuous partner-swapping. Today, it is practised globally in social settings and large international flash mobs.
profile.profile_long:
Rueda de Casino, frequently referred to simply as Rueda, is a dynamic round dance born from the Cuban dance style known as 'casino.' It was developed in Havana, Cuba, in the early 1950s, with origins traced back to approximately 1956 at the Club Casino Deportivo. The dance emerged as a novel way of interpreting Cuban Urban Son, Cuban Cha Cha Cha, Mambo, and Rumba Guaguancó in a group setting. Inspired by street dancers practicing rueda in circles, participants began forming wheels of couples who performed synchronized turns and figures.

Throughout the 1950s, Rueda de Casino spread to prominent clubs along the beachfronts and capital, including La Tropical, Los Jardines de la Tropicana, and El Liceo de la Habana. Groups of friends, family members, and professional dancers shaped its vocabulary. By the late 1970s, Rueda de Casino groups gained wider prominence via the Cuban television show 'Para Bailar.' Following the Mariel boatlift and the Castro regime, Cuban emigrants carried the tradition to Miami in the late 1980s and early 1990s, where it experienced an explosion of popularity, undergoing structural changes under teachers like Rene Gueits.

The structural framework of Rueda de Casino requires a minimum of two couples, expanding to fill whatever venue space is available. A caller—known as a cantante or líder—directs the figures aloud while actively participating as a dancer within the circle. When ambient noise drowns out voices, callers utilize hand signals, such as tapping the head for 'Sombrero.' Fundamental movements include 'al Medio,' 'Guapea,' 'Dame,' and 'Enchufla.' Over time, regional variants and hundreds of creative figures have developed, leading to massive international events such as the International Rueda de Casino Multi Flash Mob involving thousands of dancers across dozens of countries.

sections.origins_and_history: Rueda de Casino was developed in Havana, Cuba in the early 1950s, originating around 1956 at the Club Casino Deportivo. It grew out of Cuban Urban Son, Cha Cha Cha, Mambo, and Rumba Guaguancó, inspired by street dancers practicing in circular formations. It expanded through clubs like La Tropical and Los Jardines de la Tropicana, and gained television exposure in the late 1970s on 'Para Bailar.' Emigration brought it to Miami during the Mariel boatlift, sparking global dissemination.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Couples form a circle and execute synchronized figures called out by a dancing leader (cantante). The dance relies heavily on spontaneous partner-swapping, where dancers move around the circle to the next partner. It begins from 'al Medio' or 'Guapea' and incorporates fundamental moves like Dame, Enchufe, Vacila, and Sombrero, alongside complex variations and hand signals.
sections.music_and_instruments: Since the 1990s, the music most commonly used is either Salsa or a unique variation known as 'Timba.' Historically, it accompanied son montuno, guaracha, mambo, and chachachá.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditionally danced in social settings, clubs, beachfront venues, and public squares. In Havana, older founders at Jardines del 1830 are known for dressing entirely in white.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally danced among friends, family, and club members for social recreation and community bonding. It has evolved into a global phenomenon featuring massive synchronized flash mobs across hundreds of cities.
sections.notable_figures: Rene Gueits, founder of 'Salsa Lovers' in Miami (1994), structured the style. Luis Llamo ('El embajador del son') directed large-scale international record-setting rueda events in Cuba.
sections.regional_variants: Miami-style Rueda de Casino, structured and disco-like with removed folkloric elements, contrasted sharply with traditional Cuban-style Rueda. Other variants include Rueda de bachata, Swing Rueda, Rueda de Cha-cha-cha, and Roda de Kizomba.
sections.lineage: Derived from Cuban Casino, Son, Cha Cha Cha, Mambo, and Rumba Guaguancó, and has since inspired derivative round dances like Rueda de Bachata and Swing Rueda.

music_profile.sound_description: Music most commonly used is Salsa or Timba, characterized by syncopated rhythms and call-and-response structures suited for group cueing.

movement_profile.footwork: stepping forward on the inside foot and backward on the outside foot, tangent to the circle (Guapea)
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: hand signs to complement vocal calls in noisy venues
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Circular format (wheel) with multiple couples facing the center axis
movement_profile.partnering: continuous swapping of partners moving around the circle
